title: The Signature Shelf Mantel Clock
body:
Specifications (Signature design): The Signature Shelf Mantel Clock is an original Signature design for a shelf-sitting clock, 28 centimetres wide, 16 centimetres deep, and 26 centimetres tall, with a flat top, glazed front door, and four turned feet. It is a Signature original, not a copy of any maker's clock, and it runs eight days on one winding of its single spring barrel.

Mechanism: A spring barrel drives a three-wheel going train regulated by a short pendulum and an anchor escapement. The strike train sounds the hour on a coiled gong, and a silence lever on the case side lifts the hammer for quiet rooms.

Maintenance: Level the clock on its shelf with the built-in bubble on the case back, wind weekly on the same day, and dust with a soft dry cloth. Never move the clock while the pendulum swings.

Build and restoration guidance: The case is built from solid beech with a walnut veneer, and the movement plates are laid out on a Signature drilling chart so every pivot hole repeats exactly. A builder copies the chart, not an existing movement.

Tools: Soft cloth, winding key, drilling chart, spirit level.

title: Signature Tambour with Openwork Dial
body:
Specifications (Signature design): The Signature Tambour with Openwork Dial is an original Signature design: a low arched case 32 centimetres wide and 24 centimetres tall, with an openwork dial that shows the movement wheels behind the chapter ring. It runs seven days and strikes the hour on a bell. The openwork dial is a Signature design choice, not a reproduction of any historical dial.

Mechanism: A spring barrel drives the going train behind the open dial, and the short pendulum hangs below the movement. The open dial makes beat and motion visible, so the owner can see the escapement working.

Maintenance: Dust the open dial with a soft brush only, since the exposed wheels catch cloth fibres. Keep the clock level and wind weekly.

Build and restoration guidance: Cut the openwork chapter ring from brass sheet on the Signature pattern, and mount it on pillars so it never touches the wheels. Test the beat with the dial fitted, since the dial pillars can shift the movement if tightened unevenly.

Tools: Soft brush, spirit level, winding key, brass sheet pattern.

title: Signature Steeple Mantel with Glass Panels
body:
Specifications (Signature design): The Signature Steeple Mantel with Glass Panels is an original Signature design: a pointed-top case 40 centimetres tall with glazed side panels that show the pendulum and the strike train. It is shelf-sitting, with no handle and no wall bracket, and it runs eight days with hour strike on a gong.

Mechanism: A spring-driven movement with a short pendulum sits in the centre of the case, and the glass panels let the owner watch the pendulum swing and the strike train lift. The pointed top is decorative and carries a small finial.

Maintenance: Clean the glass panels with a dry soft cloth, and keep the clock level so the pendulum clears the glass. Wind weekly and check the panel catches close firmly.

Build and restoration guidance: Glaze the side panels after the movement is fitted and tested, so glass dust never reaches the wheels. Seat the movement on a Signature mounting block that holds it square to the panels.

Tools: Soft cloth, spirit level, winding key, panel catches.

title: Signature Mantel Dial with Signature Numerals
body:
Specifications (Signature design): The Signature Mantel Dial with Signature Numerals is an original Signature design: a 15-centimetre round dial whose hour marks use the Signature numeral set, with sixty minute marks and a small seconds subsidiary dial. It fits any Signature mantel movement and is never presented as a historical dial.

Mechanism: The hour wheel turns once per twelve hours and the minute wheel once per hour, geared 12 to 1, exactly as in a standard mantel dial. The Signature numerals are painted on the chapter ring only; the gearing underneath is standard clockwork.

Maintenance: Clean the dial with a dry soft brush only. If a numeral chips, touch it up from the Signature numeral chart rather than repainting the whole ring.

Build and restoration guidance: Paint the chapter ring from the Signature numeral chart, bake the paint, then fit the ring on pillars. Set the hands to twelve and the hour mark together before closing the door.

Tools: Numeral chart, soft brush, hand puller, tweezers.

title: Signature Spring Barrel with Dual Mainsprings
body:
Specifications (Signature design): The Signature Spring Barrel with Dual Mainsprings is an original Signature design: two matched mainsprings in one widened barrel, each 16 millimetres wide, sharing the load so the barrel delivers steadier torque across the week. The movement runs eight days, and the dual springs are a Signature engineering choice, not a historical pattern.

Mechanism: The two springs wind together on the same arbor and unwind together through the barrel teeth into the centre wheel. Sharing the load halves the stress on each spring, which lengthens spring life and flattens the torque curve from full wind to run-down.

Maintenance: Service dual springs only with barrel clamps and a winder rated for the pair. If one spring breaks, replace both as a matched pair, since a new spring beside a tired one unbalances the torque.

Build and restoration guidance: Wind both springs onto the arbor in the same direction and check the barrel cap seats without pinching. Log the spring pair's fitting date on the movement plate.

Tools: Mainspring winder, barrel clamps, spring grease, screwdrivers.

title: Signature Fourteen-Day Mantel Movement
body:
Specifications (Signature design): The Signature Fourteen-Day Mantel Movement is an original Signature design: a widened barrel and a slower first gearing stretch the run to fourteen days, so the clock is wound every second Sunday. The case is a standard flat-top mantel case, 30 centimetres wide, and the movement strikes the hour throughout the fortnight.

Mechanism: A longer mainspring and a barrel that turns half as fast per day give the extra week. The escapement, pendulum, and strike train are standard Signature mantel parts; only the barrel and the first wheel differ from the eight-day design.

Maintenance: Wind every fourteen days on the same weekday, turning the key steadily until resistance rises firmly. A fortnight movement that stops at ten days needs service, not harder winding.

Build and restoration guidance: Match the replacement spring to the fourteen-day specification exactly: an eight-day spring in this barrel shortens the run and confuses the owner. Stamp the barrel cap with the fourteen-day mark.

Tools: Winding key, barrel stamp, notebook for winding day.

title: Signature Short Pendulum with Temperature Rod
body:
Specifications (Signature design): The Signature Short Pendulum with Temperature Rod is an original Signature design: a 20-centimetre pendulum whose rod pairs steel with brass so expansion in one metal offsets expansion in the other, holding the effective length steadier across room temperatures. It fits any Signature mantel case with room for a short pendulum.

Mechanism: As temperature rises, the steel rod lengthens and the brass compensating section shifts the bob upward by a matching amount, so the period stays near its rated value. The anchor and suspension are standard Signature mantel parts.

Maintenance: Keep the rod clean and dry, and never oil the suspension spring. Check the rate at summer and winter room temperatures and log both, so a drift can be traced to the rod or to wear.

Build and restoration guidance: Assemble the rod pair on the Signature jig, set the bob at the chart length, and test the period at two temperatures before casing. A rod that over- or under-compensates is adjusted by moving the brass section, not by bending the rod.

Tools: Temperature jig, rating-nut key, spirit level, rate log.

title: Signature Balance Mantel for Shelves That Shake
body:
Specifications (Signature design): The Signature Balance Mantel for Shelves That Shake is an original Signature design for rooms where foot traffic shakes the shelf: a balance-wheel movement that keeps time without a pendulum, beating 21,600 vibrations per hour, or six per second. It strikes the hour on a gong and fits a flat-top mantel case.

Mechanism: A balance wheel with a hairspring oscillates on its staff and a lever escapement releases the escape wheel each vibration. With no pendulum to swing out of beat, shelf vibration changes the rate far less than it would in a pendulum clock.

Maintenance: Keep the clock away from magnets and strong shocks, and have the balance pivots oiled at service. If the clock stops after a heavy knock, check the hairspring for coils touching before assuming the movement is worn.

Build and restoration guidance: Poise the balance on the Signature poising tool and set the hairspring flat and centred before casing. Test the rate upright and tilted, since the design goal is a small difference between the two.

Tools: Timing machine, poising tool, tweezers, demagnetizer.

title: Signature Silent-Night Strike Control
body:
Specifications (Signature design): The Signature Silent-Night Strike Control is an original Signature design: a cam on the hour wheel lifts the strike hammer off its gong between ten at night and seven in the morning, so the clock keeps time silently overnight and resumes striking at seven. The going train runs all night; only the strike is silenced.

Mechanism: The night cam holds the strike locking lever engaged during the silent hours, so the strike train never releases. At seven the cam drops, the lever frees, and the next hour strikes normally. A manual override lever on the case side restores striking at any hour.

Maintenance: If the clock strikes at night, the cam has slipped on the hour wheel and needs repositioning. If it stays silent past seven, the override lever may be engaged, so check that first before opening the case.

Build and restoration guidance: Fit the cam with the hands at seven in the morning and test the silence boundary at ten at night and at seven by advancing the hands forward. Never turn the hands backwards across the boundary during testing.

Tools: Screwdrivers, tweezers, hour test chart.

title: Signature Westminster Chime with Soft Hammers
body:
Specifications (Signature design): The Signature Westminster Chime with Soft Hammers is an original Signature design: a Westminster quarter chime on four rods, with hammer heads faced in soft leather so the tone is mellow at close range on a living-room shelf. The chime barrel, rods, and hour strike follow the standard Westminster pattern, and the soft hammers are the Signature variation.

Mechanism: A pinned chime barrel lifts four hammers in the Cambridge Quarters sequence: four notes at the quarter, eight at the half, twelve at three-quarters, and sixteen at the hour, followed by the hour strike. Soft leather faces lengthen the hammer contact slightly and soften the attack.

Maintenance: Check the leather faces yearly: flattened or hardened leather brings back the harsh click the design removes. Replace faces as a set of four so the tone stays even across the rods.

Build and restoration guidance: Face the hammers on the Signature jig so all four faces meet their rods squarely, then tune the rods as a set in the finished case. Log the leather thickness on the movement plate.

Tools: Leather faces, jig, rod tuning file, soft cloth.

title: Signature Triple-Chime Selector
body:
Specifications (Signature design): The Signature Triple-Chime Selector is an original Signature design: a dial-side lever with three marked positions, Westminster, Whittington, and St Michael, plus a fourth silent position, shifting the chime barrel sideways to the chosen melody track. The selector is designed to move only when the clock is silent between chimes.

Mechanism: The barrel carries three pin tracks and the selector fork slides the barrel along its arbor so one track meets the eight hammers. A detent clicks at each position so the owner can feel the selection without looking. The silent position lifts all hammers clear of the barrel.

Maintenance: Move the selector only between chimes. If a melody plays mixed notes from two tracks, the barrel has stopped mid-shift and the selector needs reseating at its detent.

Build and restoration guidance: Map the three tracks on the Signature pin chart before fitting the barrel, and test every melody at every quarter. Adjust the detent spring so the lever clicks firmly but moves with one finger.

Tools: Pin chart, detent spring gauge, tweezers, oil pen.

title: Signature Grande Sonnerie with Hour Repeat
body:
Specifications (Signature design): The Signature Grande Sonnerie with Hour Repeat is an original Signature design: a grande sonnerie mantel clock that strikes the hour at every quarter, plus a pull cord that repeats the last hour count on demand. The repeat is a Signature addition to the grande sonnerie pattern, letting the owner hear the hour again without looking at the dial.

Mechanism: The strike train releases at every quarter and the rack sets the hour count each time. The pull cord winds a small repeat spring that replays the rack position without disturbing the going train, so the repeat never changes the time shown.

Maintenance: Wind the going and strike trains on schedule, since grande sonnerie strikes four times as often as an hour-only clock. If the repeat counts wrong, the rack has not reset, so let the next quarter strike before pulling again.

Build and restoration guidance: Test all ninety-six quarters in order, then test the repeat at six different hours before casing. The repeat cord must run free through its case hole without rubbing the pendulum.

Tools: Quarter test chart, rack gauge, oil pen, screwdrivers.

title: Signature Perpetual Calendar Mantel
body:
Specifications (Signature design): The Signature Perpetual Calendar Mantel is an original Signature design: a mantel clock whose date, day, month, and leap-year display advance mechanically without owner correction across the four-hundred-year Gregorian cycle, including the century rule that skips leap years in years divisible by one hundred but not by four hundred. The dial shows the date in an aperture and the month on a subsidiary ring.

Mechanism: A program wheel with a four-year cam and a century cam steps the date disc, skipping February 29 except in true leap years. The month ring advances at each month end, and the leap-year hand moves once per year. The calendar train runs from the hour wheel, so it needs no separate winding.

Maintenance: Never set the calendar backwards across midnight, and never force the date disc by hand. If the date skips after a service, the program wheel is one step out and must be reset to a known leap year before testing.

Build and restoration guidance: Set the program wheel to the year 2028, a leap year, and test the February 29 step, the century skip logic on the chart, and all twelve month ends before casing. Record the set year on the movement plate.

Tools: Gregorian cycle chart, tweezers, oil pen, date test log.

title: Signature Self-Leveling Mantel Case
body:
Specifications (Signature design): The Signature Self-Leveling Mantel Case is an original Signature design: a mantel case whose movement cradle pivots on two side pins and settles level under its own weight, so a shelf that slopes by up to three degrees still leaves the pendulum in beat. The case itself sits flat on its feet; only the cradle inside moves.

Mechanism: The cradle hangs from pins set above the movement's centre of gravity, so gravity pulls it to level like a ship's gimbal. A soft stop limits the swing to three degrees each way, and the pendulum hangs from the cradle, not from the case, so it inherits the level.

Maintenance: Keep the cradle pins clean and lightly oiled, and check the cradle swings freely by tilting the case slightly and watching it return. If the cradle sticks, dust or a bent pin is the cause, not the movement.

Build and restoration guidance: Balance the cradle on the Signature jig before fitting the movement, and set the stops at exactly three degrees with a protractor. Test the beat with the case tilted two degrees each way before delivery.

Tools: Protractor, jig, oil pen, spirit level.

title: Signature Tool-Free Service Mantel Movement
body:
Specifications (Signature design): The Signature Tool-Free Service Mantel Movement is an original Signature design: a mantel movement whose plates are held by captive thumb screws and whose barrel cap, pallets, and pendulum suspension lift out by hand, so a full strip-down for cleaning needs no screwdriver. The design goal is a service interval of seven years with a strip-down any careful owner can do.

Mechanism: Captive screws stay in the plates when loosened, so no screw is lost during service. The going barrel slides out on guide rails, and the escapement bridge lifts as one unit with its pallets set, so the beat setting survives a cleaning and the clock needs no re-beating afterwards.

Maintenance: At seven years, loosen the thumb screws, lift the barrel and bridges, clean in clock solution, re-oil the twelve marked oil points, and refit in reverse order. Log the service date on the case back card.

Build and restoration guidance: Build the movement on the Signature service jig so every captive screw lines up with its plate hole. Test that the movement runs for seven days uncased after reassembly before returning it to the case.

Tools: No screwdriver needed; clock solution, fine oiler, service log card.

title: Signature Auto-Beat Mantel Regulator
body:
Specifications (Signature design): The Signature Auto-Beat Mantel Regulator is an original Signature design: a mantel regulator whose crutch carries a small gravity arm that nudges the escapement toward even beat whenever the tick and tock drift apart. The owner sets the beat once, and the arm corrects small drifts from shelf bumps and seasonal wood movement without opening the case.

Mechanism: The gravity arm hangs from the crutch pivot and rests lightly against a beat screw. When the swing is uneven, the arm's weight biases the crutch back toward centre by a fraction of a millimetre per day, so the beat error shrinks over days rather than in one jump. Rate is still set separately by the rating nut.

Maintenance: Listen monthly: an even tick-tock means the arm is doing its work. If the beat error grows instead of shrinking, the arm pivot is dry or the arm is bent, and a service should free it before any regulation is attempted.

Build and restoration guidance: Fit the arm on the Signature beat jig, set the initial beat by ear, then run the movement for fourteen days and log the beat error daily. The design passes when the error falls below one percent without hand adjustment.

Tools: Beat jig, timing machine, rating-nut key, beat log.
